questions.topic: A B flat clarinet part read at concert pitch
questions.learningObjective: convert written pitches of a B flat clarinet part into sounding pitches
questions.stem: A clarinet in B flat is given a part in 4/4, common time, notated in g major. The bar holds a written B4 quarter note, a written C5 quarter note and a written D5 quarter note, which fills the bar exactly. What does the clarinet actually sound, and what concert key do those pitches belong to?

options.text: The clarinet sounds B4, C5 and D5 exactly as written, because the flute, oboe and bassoon family are read straight from the part at concert pitch
options.misconception: believes a B flat clarinet is notated at concert pitch

options.text: The clarinet sounds A4, Bb4 and C5, each a tone below its written pitch, and all three belong to concert f major, which is the key the written g major part stands for
The clarinet sounds A3, Bb3 and C4, a tone and an octave below written, because every clarinet in B flat is treated as an octave-transposing instrument like the double bass
options.misconception: adds the double bass octave displacement to the B flat transposition

options.text: The clarinet sounds C5, D5 and E5, a tone above written, because a part in B flat is written higher than it sounds rather than lower
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the B flat transposition

questions.explanation: A B flat instrument is notated a whole tone above the pitch it produces, so every written note comes down two semitones to sound. Written B4 falls to A4, written C5 falls to Bb4, and written D5 falls to C5, three semitones each. The bar is notated in g major, which has one sharp, and the concert key of such a part always sits a whole tone below its written key: a written g major is a sounding f major, which has one flat. The check is that all three sounding pitches are members of f major. A4, Bb4 and C5 are, and none of them needs an accidental in f major. The trap in the second option is real but belongs to a different family: the double bass is the orchestral instrument that is written an octave above sounding, and a bass clarinet in B flat adds an octave below but not a whole tone of extra distance.
questions.hint: Bring every written note down a whole tone, then check the resulting three pitches against f major.

questions.topic: The frequency of a B flat trumpet note at concert A3
questions.learningObjective: compute the frequency in hertz of a transposed concert pitch
questions.stem: A trumpet in B flat is given a written quarter note on E4 in 4/4, common time, in concert f major. The written note sounds a whole tone lower, so the sounding pitch is A3. Taking A4 as 440 hertz in equal temperament, what is the frequency of that sounding A3 in hertz, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: A3 lies exactly one octave below A4, and in equal temperament an octave is a doubling of frequency, so the answer is half of 440, which is 220.00 hertz. The equal-temperament formula is f = 440 x 2 to the power of (n - 69) divided by 12, with n the MIDI note number, and A3 has n = 57, giving 440 x 2 to the power of -1 and therefore 220.00. A second route reaches the same figure: the C an octave and a sixth below the A4 reference, C3, is 130.81 hertz, and A3 is a major sixth above C3, a factor of 2 to the power of 9 divided by 12, which is 1.68179, and 130.81 times 1.68179 is 220.00. The trap is 233.08, which is A3 calculated as a minor third above G3 read at 207.65 instead of a major sixth, and 440.00, which is the reference itself rather than an octave below it.
questions.hint: A3 is one octave below the 440 hertz reference, and an octave doubles the frequency.

questions.topic: An F horn part read at concert pitch
questions.learningObjective: convert written pitches of an F horn part into sounding pitches
questions.stem: A horn in F is given a part in 4/4, common time, notated in c major. The bar holds a written G4 half note and a written E4 half note, which fills the bar exactly. What does the horn actually sound, and how do those two pitches relate to the concert key?

options.text: The horn sounds C4 and then A3, a perfect fifth below each written pitch, and both belong to concert f major, the key a written c major part stands for in F
The horn sounds G4 and then E4 exactly as written, because the horn is a brass instrument and brass parts are read at concert pitch
options.misconception: believes all brass parts are notated at concert pitch

options.text: The horn sounds D4 and then B3, a perfect fourth below written, because an F instrument is transposed down a perfect fourth rather than a perfect fifth
options.misconception: transposes an F instrument by a fourth instead of a fifth

options.text: The horn sounds C5 and then A4, a perfect fifth above written, because a horn part is written a fifth below the pitch it produces
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the F transposition

questions.explanation: The name of a transposing instrument states the pitch it sounds when a written C4 is read. A horn in F therefore sounds F4 when the part shows a written C4, which places every written note a perfect fifth, or seven semitones, below its sounding pitch. Written G4 falls to C4 and written E4 falls to A3, and the interval between the two sounding notes, A3 up to C4, is a minor third of three semitones, the same minor third as the written E4 to G4. Because the part is notated in c major, the concert key is f major, one step down the circle of fifths, and both C4 and A3 are members of f major. The trap in the second option is a genuine confusable: an instrument in G transposes down a perfect fourth, so the fourth is the distance associated with a G instrument rather than an F one.
questions.hint: An instrument in F sounds F4 for a written C4, so drop every written note by a perfect fifth.

questions.topic: How far an F english horn sounds below its written note
questions.learningObjective: measure the sounding distance of an english horn in F
questions.stem: An english horn in F plays a written dotted half note on Bb4 in 3/4, simple triple metre, in concert e flat major. By how many semitones below the written Bb4 does the sounding pitch lie, and what is that sounding pitch's scientific pitch name?
questions.explanation: An english horn in F is a transposing woodwind, and the F in its name means it produces F4 when the part shows a written C4, so every written note falls a perfect fifth to reach its sounding pitch. A perfect fifth is seven semitones, so the distance asked for is 7. The spelling of the sounding pitch comes from the letters rather than from the semitone count, because a written Bb4 remains a Bb4 whatever an instrument does with it, and a fifth below the letter B is the letter E, so the sounding pitch of a written Bb4 is Eb4. Two checks confirm the pair. Eb4 has note number 63 and Bb4 has 70, and 70 minus 63 is 7, and Eb4 is the tonic of the stated concert key of e flat major, which has three flats, so the sounding note lands inside the harmony. The bar arithmetic is consistent too, since a dotted half note is three quarter-note beats and 3/4 holds three. The traps are 2, the distance a B flat instrument falls, and 14, which a bass clarinet in B flat falls because it adds an octave to that same tone.
questions.hint: An F instrument sounds a perfect fifth below written, and a perfect fifth is seven semitones.

questions.topic: A D trumpet part read at concert pitch
questions.learningObjective: convert written pitches of a D trumpet part into sounding pitches
questions.stem: A trumpet in D is given a part in 4/4, common time, notated in c major. The bar holds a written C5 whole note, which fills the bar exactly. What does the trumpet actually sound, and what key does that pitch establish?

options.text: The trumpet sounds C5 exactly as written, because a trumpet part in D is only a different crook on an instrument that still reads at concert pitch
options.misconception: treats a D trumpet as a non-transposing instrument

options.text: The trumpet sounds Bb4, a major second below written, because every trumpet part is written a tone above the pitch it sounds
options.misconception: applies the B flat trumpet transposition to a D trumpet

options.text: The trumpet sounds F5, a perfect fourth above written, because the letter D in the instrument name counts four steps up the staff rather than two semitones
options.misconception: reads the instrument name as a staff distance rather than a sounding pitch

options.text: The trumpet sounds D5, a major second above its written C5, and the bar establishes concert d major, the key a written c major part stands for in D, with D5 as that key's tonic

questions.explanation: The letter after a transposing instrument's name is the pitch it sounds when the part shows a written C4. A trumpet in D therefore produces D4 for a written C4, and the same relation holds at every octave, so a written C5 produces D5, a major second or two semitones above. D trumpets are rare, but the same convention governs the piccolo in D flat, which sounds a minor sixth below written, and they exist because the tubing is easier to make at certain lengths. The written key is c major and the concert key is a whole tone higher, so d major, and D5 is its fifth degree. The direction is the thing to be careful about: a D instrument sounds higher, because the sounding D4 is a second above the written C4, while a B flat instrument sounds lower, because the sounding Bb4 is a second below the written C4.
questions.hint: A D instrument sounds D4 for a written C4, which is a second above, not below.

questions.topic: The frequency of a horn note once a crook is fitted
questions.learningObjective: compute a sounding frequency after an instrument is crooked up
questions.stem: A horn in F is given a new crook that makes the instrument sound a perfect fourth higher than it did before, so it now behaves as an instrument in B flat alto. The part stays in 4/4, common time, and is still notated in written c major, and the horn plays a written half note on C5. Taking A4 as 440 hertz, what is the frequency in hertz of the sounding pitch, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: The crook raises the instrument's sounding pitch by a perfect fourth, which is five semitones, so a written C5 that produced F4 on the uncroked horn produces Bb4 on the crooked one. That is consistent with the new identity of the instrument: a crook in B flat on an F horn turns it into a horn in B flat alto, and a B flat alto horn sounds a major second below its written pitch, so written C5 gives Bb4. Bb4 has MIDI note number 70, and the equal-temperament formula 440 x 2 to the power of (70 - 69) divided by 12 gives 440 x 2 to the 1 divided by 12, a factor of 1.059463, and the product is 466.16 hertz. As a check from below, the uncroked sounding pitch F4 is 349.23 hertz, and five semitones is a factor of 2 to the power of 5 divided by 12, which is 1.334840, and 349.23 times 1.334840 is 466.16. The trap is 392.00, which is G4 and would be the result of raising the written C5 by a fourth instead of lowering the sounding pitch.
questions.hint: Raise the uncrooked sounding F4 by a perfect fourth and convert the resulting Bb4 to hertz.

questions.topic: Tracing the rule that converts a written part to concert pitch
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that subtracts an instrument shift from written note numbers
questions.stem: Trace the rule concert(written, shift), which returns the sounding note number of a written note for an instrument that sounds shift semitones below what is printed: concert(written, shift) = return note(written) - shift, where note() is the MIDI number of the pitch name. Apply it with shift = 7, the value for a horn in F, to a part in 4/4, common time, notated in c major, containing a written C5 half note, a written G4 half note and a written A4 quarter note followed by a written B4 quarter note. What three sounding pitches does the rule return?

options.text: C5, then G4, then A4, since the rule returns the written note unchanged whenever the shift is an exact number of semitones
options.misconception: believes an integral shift leaves the written pitch unchanged

options.text: D5, then B4, then C5, since the rule adds the shift instead of subtracting it, so 72 plus 7 is 79 and 67 plus 7 is 74
options.misconception: adds the shift rather than subtracting it

options.text: F4, then C4, then D4, since note(C5) is 72, note(G4) is 67 and note(A4) is 69, and 72 minus 7 is 65, 67 minus 7 is 60 and 69 minus 7 is 62
F4, then C4, then Bb3, since note(B4) is 71 and the rule returns 71 minus 7 as 64, a pitch the caller must read as Bb3
options.misconception: reads note 64 as Bb3 when it is E4 in scientific pitch notation

questions.explanation: The rule is subtraction, and the first job is to attach a number to each written pitch name. In scientific pitch notation and MIDI numbering, C4 is 60, so the written C5 is 72, the written G4 is 67, the written A4 is 69 and the written B4 is 71. Subtracting the shift of 7 gives 65, 60 and 62 for the first three notes, and 71 minus 7 is 64 for the fourth. Converting back to names, 65 is F4, 60 is C4, 62 is D4 and 64 is E4. All four belong to f major, which is the concert key of a written c major horn part, and that is the check that the trace went the right way. The trap in the third option is a numbering error rather than an arithmetic one: MIDI note 64 is E4, since 60 is C4 and 64 is four semitones above it, and 64 minus nothing is not Bb3, which is 58.
questions.hint: Convert each pitch name to a number first, subtract seven, then convert the results back to names.

questions.topic: The written note that produces a given concert pitch in a B flat part
questions.learningObjective: invert a transposition to find the written note for a concert pitch
questions.stem: An oboe and a clarinet in B flat are playing the same concert passage in 4/4, common time, in concert c major. The conductor wants a sounding C5 on the beat. What does the oboe read and what does the clarinet read, and how do the two notations keep the same sounding result?

options.text: The oboe reads a written C5 and the clarinet also reads a written C5, because both instruments are notated from the same sounding concert part
options.misconception: assumes a transposing part is copied unchanged from a concert part

options.text: The oboe reads a written C5 quarter note and the clarinet reads a written D5 quarter note, because the clarinet's part is printed a whole tone high so that its D5 produces the oboe's C5
The oboe reads a written C5 and the clarinet reads a written Bb4, because a B flat instrument is written a whole tone below the pitch it sounds
options.misconception: subtracts the transposition instead of adding it to reach the written note

options.text: The oboe reads a written G4 and the clarinet reads a written C5, because the oboe sounds an octave above its written pitch in the same way the piccolo does
options.misconception: gives the oboe the piccolo octave displacement

questions.explanation: Finding the written note for a given sounding pitch means running the transposition backwards, and the direction reverses. A B flat clarinet sounds a whole tone below what is printed, so to obtain a sounding C5 the part must show the note two semitones above it, which is D5. The oboe is not a transposing instrument, so its printed C5 is the concert C5 and needs no adjustment. Both notations therefore differ on the page by a whole tone, and both produce the identical sounding result, which is the whole point of the convention: every player reads a line that lies in a comfortable register for their instrument while the sounding music stays the same. The arithmetic check is symmetric. Converting the clarinet's written D5 down two semitones gives C5, and converting the oboe's written C5 through a shift of zero gives C5. The trap in the second option is exactly this reversal, and it is the commonest error in the whole subject, because the arithmetic of transposition is addition in one direction and subtraction in the other.
questions.hint: Work backwards: a B flat clarinet sounds two semitones low, so its part must show a note two semitones above the target.

questions.topic: Tracing the rule that places a piccolo an octave up
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that adds twelve to a written note number
questions.stem: Trace the rule sounding(w), the rule for a piccolo part, which returns the note number of the pitch a piccolo produces: sounding(w) = return note(w) + 12. Apply it to a bar in 6/8, compound duple metre, notated in e major, holding a written E4 dotted quarter note and a written G#4 eighth note, which fill the bar exactly. What two sounding pitches does the rule return?

options.text: E5 and then G#5, since note(E4) is 64 and note(G#4) is 68, and 64 plus 12 is 76 while 68 plus 12 is 80
E4 and then G#4, since the rule returns the written note unchanged for an instrument that is notated at concert pitch
options.misconception: treats the piccolo as a non-transposing instrument

options.text: E6 and then G#6, since the rule adds twelve twice, once for the octave and once for the note number of the octave above
options.misconception: applies the two-octave displacement of the glockenspiel

options.text: E3 and then G#3, since the rule adds twelve to a note number and a note number counts upward from the top of the keyboard
options.misconception: assumes note numbers run downward from the top of the keyboard

questions.explanation: A piccolo is an octave-transposing instrument: its part is written in the treble clef at the octave below the pitch it produces, so the rule adds exactly twelve to the written note number. E4 has the note number 64 and G#4 has 68, so the additions give 76 and 80, which are E5 and G#5. The bar is notated in e major, which has four sharps, and both written pitches E and G# are in that key, and the sounding pitches E5 and G#5 are in the same key because an octave displacement does not change a pitch class. The trap in the second option confuses two octave-transposing instruments: the glockenspiel is written two octaves below sounding, so it needs twenty-four added, while the piccolo and the celesta need twelve and the xylophone also needs twelve. The trap in the third option misreads the direction of MIDI numbering, which rises from the bottom of the keyboard and not from the top.
questions.hint: Twelve is one octave in note numbers, and the piccolo needs one octave, not two.

questions.topic: The frequency of a glockenspiel note two octaves above written
questions.learningObjective: compute a sounding frequency after a two-octave displacement
questions.stem: A glockenspiel part in 4/4, common time, notated in e major, has a written half note on A4. A glockenspiel sounds two octaves above its written pitch, so the sounding note is A6. Taking A4 as 440 hertz in equal temperament, what is the frequency of the sounding A6 in hertz, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: Two octaves is a factor of four in frequency, because each octave doubles and two doublings give 2 x 2 = 4, so 440 x 4 is 1760.00 hertz. The formula route gives the same figure: A6 has the note number 93, and 440 x 2 to the power of (93 - 69) divided by 12 is 440 x 2 to the power of 2, which is 440 x 4. A third route climbs the series: A4 at 440.00, A5 at 880.00, A6 at 1760.00, each step a doubling. The check is the note number, since A4 is 69, each octave adds twelve, so A5 is 81 and A6 is 93, and 93 minus 69 is 24, exactly two octaves of twelve semitones. The glockenspiel's written range is a second reason the two-octave displacement is used, because its bars are short and the written part then fits on the treble staff without going far above it. The traps are 880.00, which is only one octave up and belongs to the piccolo and the celesta, and 3520.00, which is three octaves up.
questions.hint: Each octave doubles the frequency, so two octaves multiply the 440 hertz reference by four.

questions.topic: The double bass octave displacement
questions.learningObjective: convert written double bass pitches into sounding pitches
questions.stem: A double bass part in 4/4, common time, notated in c major, holds a written G2 half note and a written C3 half note, which fill the bar exactly. What does the double bass actually sound, and which written clef does its part use?

options.text: The double bass sounds G2 and then C3 exactly as written, because the bass clef already places the part an octave lower than the treble clef does
options.misconception: believes a change of clef displaces the sounding octave

options.text: The double bass sounds G3 and then C4, an octave above written, because a part written in the bass clef is notated a ninth higher than it sounds
options.misconception: reverses the octave displacement of the double bass

options.text: The double bass sounds G1 and then C2 but its part is written in the treble clef, because the treble clef is the only clef used for a string instrument
options.misconception: assigns the treble clef to the double bass

options.text: The double bass sounds G1 and then C2, each an octave below its written pitch, and its part is written in the bass clef because that keeps the notes near the middle of the staff

questions.explanation: The double bass is the one orchestral string instrument whose part is not written at sounding pitch, and it is written a full octave above the sound it makes. Written G2 therefore produces G1 and written C3 produces C2, both an octave, or twelve semitones, lower. The reason is physical and not merely conventional: the vibrating length of the instrument's longest string is close to a metre, and at that length the overtones are widely spaced, so a family of higher strings would be needed to fill the range. Writing the part an octave up lets the player use the shorter strings that actually exist. Its part is written in the bass clef, and the written notes G2 and C3 sit on the bottom line and the second space of that staff, which is comfortable to read. The trap in the second option is the direction: a clef change moves a note across the staff but never changes its sounding pitch, and only the octave displacement does that.
questions.hint: The double bass is written an octave above sounding, and its part uses the bass clef.

questions.topic: Tracing the rule for a bass clarinet in B flat
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that combines a tone transposition with an octave displacement
questions.stem: Trace the rule sounding(w) for a bass clarinet in B flat, which returns the note number of the pitch produced: sounding(w) = return note(w) - 14. The rule subtracts a whole tone for the B flat naming and twelve more for the octave below the treble clarinet. Apply it to a bar in 4/4, common time, notated in f major, holding a written F4 half note, a written A4 quarter note and a written C5 quarter note. What three sounding pitches does the rule return?

options.text: F4, then A4, then C5, since a bass clarinet in B flat is a non-transposing instrument whose part is copied straight from the concert score
options.misconception: ignores both the tone and the octave of the bass clarinet

options.text: F3, then A3, then C4, since note(F4) is 65 and the rule returns 65 minus 14 as 51, a number the caller must read as F3
options.misconception: reads note 51 as F3 when it is Eb3

options.text: Eb3, then G3, then Bb3, since note(F4) is 65, note(A4) is 69 and note(C5) is 72, and 65 minus 14 is 51, 69 minus 14 is 55 and 72 minus 14 is 58
Gb3, then Ab3, then Bb3, since a B flat instrument is named for the note it sounds and so turns a written C4 into a written Bb4
options.misconception: renames every written pitch after the instrument name

questions.explanation: Fourteen semitones is a whole tone of B flat naming plus an octave, and the trace is three subtractions followed by three conversions. The written F4, A4 and C5 have note numbers 65, 69 and 72. Subtracting fourteen gives 51, 55 and 58. Converting back, 51 is Eb3, 55 is G3 and 58 is Bb3, because C4 is 60 and each of these sits below it by the right count. The key check confirms the direction: the part is notated in f major, and a B flat bass clarinet sounds a whole tone lower, so the concert key is e flat major, and Eb3, G3 and Bb3 are all members of e flat major, which has three flats. The trap in the second option is a numbering slip, since 51 is Eb3 and not F3, and F3 would be 53. The trap in the third option is a real misreading of the naming convention, but the letter in an instrument's name is the pitch produced for a written C4 and is not a template to be stamped over every other note.
questions.hint: Subtract fourteen from each written note number, then convert the results back to pitch names and check them against e flat major.

questions.topic: Reading four woodwind parts at the same written pitch
questions.learningObjective: identify which woodwind instruments sound the written pitch
questions.stem: In 4/4, common time, in concert c major, four players are each given the same written pitch, a C5 half note followed by a D5 half note. The players are an oboe, a flute, a bassoon and a clarinet in B flat. Which of the four sound the written pitch, and which does not?

options.text: Only the oboe sounds the written pitch, since the flute and the bassoon both use parts written in the treble clef an octave away from sounding
options.misconception: believes a clef choice changes the sounding octave

options.text: The oboe, the flute and the bassoon all sound C5 and D5 as written, while the clarinet in B flat sounds Bb4 and C5, a whole tone lower than the part shows
The flute and the oboe sound the written pitch, while the bassoon sounds a whole tone lower, since a bassoon is named for the B flat it sounds
options.misconception: reads the bass in bassoon as a B flat naming

options.text: All four sound the written pitch, since the four staves are the same length and a bar of the same metre must contain the same pitches
options.misconception: infers sounding pitch from the shape of the stave

questions.explanation: Three of these four instruments are notated at sounding pitch, and the deciding test is whether the instrument's name carries a transposing letter. The flute, oboe and bassoon are all in C, meaning they produce a written C4 as a sounding C4, and each is simply named for the note it produces rather than for its tube length or its family. The clarinet in B flat is the exception in this group, and it sounds a whole tone below its part, so its written C5 and D5 reach the ear as Bb4 and C5. The check that the three non-transposing parts really do agree is that the concert key of all four readings is c major, which is what the bar of C5 and D5 belongs to. The trap in the first option confuses a clef with a transposition: choosing the bass clef or the treble clef for a part changes where a note sits on the page and never changes what pitch sounds.
questions.hint: A transposing instrument has a letter in its name; the flute, oboe and bassoon are all in C.

questions.topic: The bottom line of the treble staff
questions.learningObjective: name the pitch on a given line of a given clef
questions.stem: A violin part in 4/4, common time, in g major, has a note placed on the bottom line of the treble staff, written as a quarter note. What is the scientific pitch name of that line, and what is the reason?

options.text: The bottom line is E4, because the treble clef fixes its curl on the second line, which is G4, and counting down the five lines and four spaces from G4 gives E4
The bottom line is G4, because the treble clef names G4 and a clef names the bottom line of the staff it is attached to
options.misconception: believes a clef names the bottom line rather than the line its symbol curls around

options.text: The bottom line is C4, because middle C always sits on the bottom line of whichever staff it is written on
options.misconception: places middle C on the bottom line of every staff

options.text: The bottom line is F4, because the spaces of the treble staff are F4, A4, C5 and E5 and the bottom line continues that list
options.misconception: reads the bottom line as the lowest named space of the staff

questions.explanation: A clef works by fixing one reference pitch on one line, and the rest of the staff follows from the rule that adjacent staff positions move by one letter name. The treble clef, a G clef, curls around the second line from the bottom, and that line is G4. Counting downward from G4: the space below it is F4, the first line is E4, the space below that is D4, and the ledger line below the staff is middle C, C4. So the bottom line is E4, and in g major, which has one sharp, E4 needs no accidental. The trap in the third option is the useful one to check, because the spaces of the treble staff really are F4, A4, C5 and E5, and the bottom line continues the same letter sequence underneath the first space, giving E4 rather than F4. questions.stem: A cello part in 4/4, common time, in d major, climbs high enough that the composer rewrites the last four bars in the tenor clef instead of the bass clef. Which line carries middle C in the tenor clef, and what does the change achieve for the player?

options.misconception: gives the tenor clef the alto clef line and confuses clef with technique

options.text: Middle C sits on the fourth line in the tenor clef, and the change pulls the high notes down onto the staff so the player reads them without ledger lines above
Middle C sits on the fourth line in the tenor clef, but the change only affects the look of the page and leaves the sounding pitches unaltered
options.misconception: misses that the clef change removes ledger lines rather than altering pitch

options.text: Middle C sits on the first line in the tenor clef, and the change lets the player read the high notes with the same fingering as the low ones

In the tenor clef the staff lines are D3, F3, A3, C4 and E4, so a cello's high register, up around D4, F4 and A4, falls inside the five lines instead of needing a stack of ledger lines above the bass staff. questions.learningObjective: apply an octave line to the notes it covers only
questions.stem: A flute part in 4/4, common time, in g major, is printed with an 8va bracket above the staff. The bracket covers a written C5 quarter note and a written D5 quarter note, then stops. The next two notes, a written E5 half note, are outside the bracket. What do the three notes sound, and what does the stopping of the bracket mean?

options.text: The C5 and D5 sound as C6 and D6, an octave above the page, and the written E5 then sounds as E5 because the bracket has stopped and no octave shift applies to it
The C5 and D5 sound as C6 and D6, and the E5 also sounds as E6, because an 8va bracket placed above the staff applies to the rest of the bar

options.text: The C5 and D5 sound as C6 and D6, and the E5 is written as E6 so that it continues the raised register in the same octave

options.misconception: reads the 8va bracket as a dynamic hairpin

The bracket's extent is part of its meaning, and it ends where the composer wants the raised register to end, so the written E5 outside it sounds as the plain E5 that is on the page. questions.topic: The 2nd partial of a harmonic series
questions.learningObjective: identify the interval of the 2nd partial above a fundamental
questions.stem: A string is stopped so that its fundamental is C2, a pitch of 65.41 hertz in equal temperament with A4 at 440 hertz. Its 2nd partial sounds at 130.81 hertz. What is that partial, spelled with an octave, and why does every string produce it?

options.text: The 2nd partial is G3, a perfect twelfth above the fundamental, because the third vibration loop is the one a violin player gets by stopping the string at its centre
options.misconception: confuses the 2nd partial with the 3rd, which gives the twelfth

options.text: The 2nd partial is C3 but only on stopped strings, because a bowed or plucked string produces its even partials only when a finger is placed on it
options.misconception: thinks even partials require a stopped string

options.text: The 2nd partial is C4, two octaves above the fundamental, because partials are counted in octaves rather than in vibration loops
options.misconception: numbers the partials by octave rather than by loop

options.text: The 2nd partial is C3, a perfect octave above the C2 fundamental, and it is present on every string because a string vibrating in two loops has its nodes at the centre and both ends

questions.explanation: A partial is counted by the number of times the string vibrates each cycle, and the 2nd partial is the string swinging in two loops, with a node at its centre and at both ends, which is exactly the shape a string takes when it is lightly touched at its midpoint. The frequency of the 2nd partial is twice the fundamental, so a C2 at 65.41 hertz gives a 2nd partial of 130.81 hertz, and doubling a frequency is a perfect octave, so the 2nd partial is C3. Every string produces it because a string has no mechanism that suppresses even partials: the shape of a vibrating string is a standing wave, and any standing wave that fits an integer number of loops can be excited to some degree. That last point is what makes the higher partials interesting, because the odd ones, the 3rd, 5th and 7th, are usually much stronger than the even ones on a bowed string, and on a stopped wooden pipe only the odd ones sound at all. The trap in the first option is the counting slip, since the fifth above the fundamental is the 3rd partial, not the 2nd.
questions.hint: The 2nd partial has twice the fundamental frequency, and doubling a frequency is an octave.

questions.topic: Reading a table of partial frequencies for a fundamental
questions.learningObjective: match a list of frequencies to the partial numbers of a harmonic series
questions.stem: An instrument is measured and its partials are found at 196.22, 261.63, 327.03 and 392.44 hertz, listed in rising order with the weakest component first. The fundamental is C2 at 65.41 hertz in equal temperament. Which partial numbers are these four components, and what does the table establish about the instrument?

options.text: They are the 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th partials, since 196.22 is twice 98.01 and the fundamental of the instrument is therefore G2 rather than C2
options.misconception: assumes a different fundamental to fit a lower partial number

options.text: They are the 4th, 5th, 6th and 7th partials, since a harmonic series doubles at every step and 196.22 must already be past the first doubling
options.misconception: counts from the top of the series downward

options.text: They are the 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th partials, since 196.22 is three times 65.41, 261.63 is four, 327.03 is five and 392.44 is six, so the instrument has a C2 fundamental
They are the 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th partials, but the fundamental must be A2 because the series is measured from the nearest equal-tempered pitch rather than from the true fundamental
options.misconception: snaps a series to the nearest named pitch instead of dividing

questions.explanation: The test is division, not resemblance. Take the stated C2 fundamental of 65.41 hertz and divide each measured component by it: 196.22 over 65.41 is 3.00, 261.63 over 65.41 is 4.00, 327.03 over 65.41 is 5.00 and 392.44 over 65.41 is 6.00. What the table establishes is that the series is a harmonic series with a C2 fundamental, and it also shows the pattern in the strengths: the table lists the weakest component first, and on most string instruments the 2nd partial is the weakest of the low partials, which is why the 2nd appears before the 3rd in the listing. The trap in the first option is the useful one, since 196.22 is twice 98.01 and so would fit a G2 fundamental as its 2nd partial, but then 261.63 would have to be a non-integer multiple of 98.01, and a harmonic series has no gaps.
questions.hint: Divide each measured frequency by the stated fundamental and look for whole numbers in order.

questions.stem: A string has a fundamental of C2 at 65.41 hertz in equal temperament with A4 at 440 hertz. The 4th partial of a harmonic series sounds at four times the fundamental. What is the frequency of that 4th partial in hertz, to two decimal places?

The musical significance is that the 4th partial is the first partial that agrees exactly with equal temperament, because it is a whole number of octaves above the fundamental, and every power of two in the series is exact in any temperament. The odd multiples in between are where temperaments differ, so the 3rd partial, a fifth, is about 2.0 cents sharp of the equal-tempered fifth, and the 5th partial, a third, is about 13.7 cents flat of the equal-tempered major third. The trap is 523.25, which is the 8th partial and three octaves above the fundamental.
questions.hint: Four times the fundamental, and four is two octaves, so the 4th partial is C4.

options.text: They form a perfect fourth of five semitones, because the 5th partial is a fifth of the fundamental and the 4th partial is an octave, so the gap must be a fourth
options.misconception: subtracts two differently named intervals without checking semitones

options.text: They form a major third of four semitones, and at 327.03 hertz against the equal-tempered E4 of 329.63 hertz the 5th partial is 13.7 cents narrower than an equal-tempered major third
They form a minor third of three semitones, because the 5th partial at 327.03 hertz lies below the equal-tempered E4 of 329.63 hertz and a note below a major third makes a minor one
options.misconception: treats a narrow interval as a smaller interval

options.text: They form a major third of four semitones that agrees exactly with equal temperament, because every partial of a harmonic series is a whole number of equal-tempered steps
options.misconception: assumes a harmonic series matches equal temperament

questions.explanation: The gap between the 4th and 5th partials is 5 minus 4, which is one unit of the fundamental, and the fundamental C2 is 65.41 hertz, so the gap is about 65.41 hertz. The 4th partial is C4 at 261.63 hertz, so the 5th partial is one fundamental above it, at 327.03 hertz, and the letter that sits a third above C is E. The size is four semitones, which is a major third, and the size is fixed by the arithmetic: 5 over 4 is 1.25, and 1.25 is the pure major third's ratio. What differs from equal temperament is the width, because the 5th partial of a C string sounds at 386.3 cents above the C4, and the equal-tempered major third is 400 cents, so the 5th partial is 13.7 cents narrow. This matters in practice, and it is the reason a string's natural third sounds slightly flatter than a keyboard's third, and why an unaccompanied string choir singing in just intonation pulls its thirds down. The trap in the second option is a real confusion to name: an interval that is too narrow is still a major third in equal-tempered notation, it is simply out of tune.

questions.topic: Which partials land within three cents of an equal-tempered pitch
questions.learningObjective: select the partials that equal temperament can place exactly
questions.stem: Four partials of a stringed C2 are measured at 130.81, 196.22, 261.63 and 327.03 hertz, and the equal-tempered reference is A4 at 440 hertz. Which of these four statements about them is true? Select every statement that holds.

options.text: The 2nd and the 4th lie within one cent of their equal-tempered notes, because a power of two in the series is a whole number of octaves and octaves are exact in every temperament
The 2nd, the 3rd and the 4th all lie within one cent of their equal-tempered notes, because a harmonic series is the set of ratios a keyboard was designed from
options.misconception: assumes equal temperament copies the harmonic series

options.text: The 2nd and the 3rd lie within one cent of their equal-tempered notes, because a fifth is the interval a well-made keyboard can also make pure
options.misconception: assumes a well-made keyboard makes its fifths pure

options.text: None of the four lies within one cent, because a string and a keyboard can never agree on any pitch at all
options.misconception: overstates the disagreement between a string and a keyboard

questions.explanation: Equal temperament places its twelve notes at exact multiples of a twelfth root of 2, and a partial of a harmonic series lands on one of those notes only when the partial number is a power of two, because powers of two are whole numbers of octaves and every temperament makes octaves exact. The 2nd partial is C3 at 130.81 hertz and the 4th is C4 at 261.63 hertz, and both fall on their equal-tempered notes with no error at all, so within one cent is easy for them. The 3rd partial at 196.22 hertz is the near miss, and it is 2.0 cents above the equal-tempered G3, which is outside a one-cent bound even though it is the closest a non-power-of-two ever comes. The 5th partial at 327.03 hertz is 13.7 cents below the equal-tempered E4, and no amount of care would bring it inside one cent. The one-cent bound is deliberately tight so that the 3rd partial's small 2.0 cents reads as a real failure rather than as a rounding matter, and that is the pedagogically useful point: a string's fifths are nearly pure, its thirds are audibly flat by 13.7 cents, and only its octaves are exact. The trap in the second option is the belief that a keyboard was derived from string partials, when the twelve-note system was chosen so that no key would be badly served.
questions.hint: Only the powers of two in the series give whole octaves, and only octaves are exact in every temperament.

questions.topic: The 11th partial and its distance from the octave
questions.learningObjective: compute a partial frequency and express it in cents above the octave
questions.stem: The 11th partial of a string whose fundamental is C2 at 65.41 hertz sounds at 719.47 hertz, with A4 at 440 hertz as the reference. The note C5, three octaves above the fundamental, has a frequency of 523.25 hertz. How many cents is that partial above the C5?
questions.explanation: The ratio of the 11th partial to C5 is 11 over 8, which is 1.375, and a ratio's size in cents is 1200 x log2 of the ratio, so the figure wanted is 1200 x log2 of 1.375, which is 1200 x 0.45943 and comes to 551.3 cents. Two independent routes agree. The first measures from the 4th partial instead, which is C4 at 261.63 hertz: the ratio 11 over 4 is 2.75, which is 1751.3 cents, and removing the 1200 cents of the octave C4 to C5 leaves 551.3 cents above C5. The second compares with equal temperament, where 551.3 cents falls 48.7 cents short of the 600 cents of an equal-tempered tritone, which is why the 11th partial cannot be spelled exactly in a twelve-note equal-tempered system. The name of the nearest equal-tempered note is F#5 at 739.99 hertz, and the partial is 48.7 cents flat of it, and that is the fact that makes the 11th of a dominant chord sound out of tune on a string instrument while sounding correct on a keyboard. The trap is 600, which is the equal-tempered tritone rather than the harmonic one, and 1751.3, which is the same measurement taken from the wrong octave.
questions.hint: The ratio against C5 is eleven over eight, so use 1200 times the base 2 logarithm of 1.375.

questions.topic: The 13th partial and the sixth it forms
questions.learningObjective: name the sixth formed by the 13th partial and state its width
questions.stem: The 13th partial of a string whose fundamental is C2 at 65.41 hertz sounds at 850.28 hertz, with A4 at 440 hertz as the reference. What interval does that partial form above the 8th partial at 523.25 hertz, and how much narrower is it than an equal-tempered interval of the same name?

options.text: The 13th partial stands a minor sixth above the 8th partial, and at 840.5 cents it is 40.5 cents wider than an equal-tempered minor sixth
options.misconception: calls a wide sixth minor and adds the error instead of subtracting it

options.text: The 13th partial stands a perfect fifth above the 8th partial, since thirteen over eight is a ratio of 1.625 and a pure fifth is 1.5
options.misconception: reads a ratio of 1.625 as a fifth

options.text: The 13th partial stands a major sixth above the 8th partial, and at 840.5 cents it is 59.5 cents narrower than the 900 cents of an equal-tempered major sixth
The 13th partial stands a major sixth above the 8th partial, and it agrees with equal temperament because 13 is a prime number and prime partials are exact
options.misconception: believes prime partial numbers are exact in equal temperament

questions.explanation: The 8th partial of a C2 string is C5 at 523.25 hertz and the 13th partial is 850.28 hertz, so the interval between them has the ratio 13 over 8, which is 1.625. Converting to size, 1200 x log2 of 1.625 is 840.5 cents, and an equal-tempered sixth is either 800 cents for a minor sixth or 900 cents for a major sixth, so 840.5 is a sixth and it is the wider of the two. The letter settles it: the 8th partial is C, and the sixth above C is A, and A natural rather than A flat gives 9 semitones, a major sixth. The width is what makes the partial famous, because it falls 59.5 cents short of the equal-tempered major sixth, the widest of the natural partials' deviations, and that is why the thirteenth of a dominant chord sounds thin on strings. A third route confirms the figure: the nearest equal-tempered note to 850.28 hertz is G#5, and the partial is 40.5 cents above that, which is the same fact measured from the other side, since 800 plus 40.5 is 840.5. The trap in the third option is a plausible-sounding rule that does not exist; no partial number makes equal temperament exact except the powers of two.
questions.hint: The ratio is thirteen over eight, so 1200 times the base 2 logarithm of 1.625 gives 840.5 cents, which is a wide sixth.

questions.topic: A pure fifth of three to two against equal temperament
questions.learningObjective: compute how far a pure fifth departs from the equal-tempered fifth
questions.stem: A string ensemble tunes its fifths by the pure ratio, so the note a fifth above a given pitch is that pitch multiplied by three halves. Equal temperament, with A4 at 440 hertz, puts that fifth 700.0 cents up. How many cents wider than the equal-tempered fifth is the pure fifth of three to two?
questions.explanation: A cent is one hundredth of a semitone, and the size of a ratio in cents is 1200 x log2 of the ratio, so the pure fifth of three to two is 1200 x log2 of 1.5, which is 1200 x 0.58496 and comes to 701.955 cents. Subtracting the equal-tempered fifth's 700.0 cents leaves 1.955 cents, so the pure fifth is 1.955 cents wider. A check from actual frequencies makes the smallness of the figure concrete: A4 at 440.00 hertz and its pure fifth E5 at 660.00 hertz, and the equal-tempered E5 is 659.26 hertz, so the pure fifth is 0.74 hertz wider at that height. The reason the figure is so small is that a fifth is the closest interval in ordinary use to being pure, since 3 over 2 is a ratio of two small whole numbers, and this near purity is exactly why five-limit just intonation sounds consonant in open fifths and clear in thirds. The traps are 5.0 and 23.46; the first is a rough guess at the size of a noticeable interval, and the second is the Pythagorean comma, which is the accumulated error of twelve pure fifths rather than the error of one.
questions.hint: Convert the ratio three halves to cents with 1200 times log base 2, then subtract 700.

questions.topic: A pure major third of five to four against equal temperament
questions.learningObjective: compute how far a pure third departs from the equal-tempered third
questions.stem: An unaccompanied string choir tunes a C4 at 261.63 hertz and takes its third above by the pure ratio of five to four, while the equal-tempered third with A4 at 440 hertz would sound E4 at 329.63 hertz. How many cents narrower than the equal-tempered major third is the pure major third?
questions.explanation: The pure third of five to four measures 1200 x log2 of 1.25 cents, which is 1200 x 0.32193 and comes to 386.314 cents, and the equal-tempered major third is exactly 400 cents, so the pure third is 400 minus 386.314, which is 13.686 cents narrower. The frequency check is the one a singer would actually hear: a C4 at 261.63 hertz times five quarters is 327.03 hertz, and the equal-tempered E4 is 329.63 hertz, so the two thirds beat against each other at 2.60 hertz, which is inside the range of beats a listener hears as roughness rather than as separate pulses. A third route gives the same number from the harmonic series, because the 5th partial of a C string is 386.3 cents above its C4, and the string's natural third is the pure third. The size of the figure is the important part, because 13.7 cents is roughly the smallest pitch difference most listeners can reliably hear in isolation, which is why a string choir singing in tune sounds obviously different from a keyboard and why the effect disappears in a full texture. The trap is 1.955, the figure for a fifth, because thirds are where the compromise bites.
questions.hint: The pure third of five to four is 386.314 cents, so subtract that from the 400 cents of an equal-tempered major third.

questions.topic: A pure minor third of six to five against equal temperament
questions.learningObjective: compute how far a pure minor third departs from the equal-tempered third
questions.stem: An A3 at 220.00 hertz is given a minor third above it by the pure ratio of six to five, while equal temperament with A4 at 440 hertz would place that third at 277.18 hertz. How many cents wider than the equal-tempered minor third is the pure minor third?

The frequency check is direct: an A3 at 220.00 hertz times six fifths is 264.00 hertz, and the equal-tempered C#4 is 277.18 hertz, so the difference is 13.18 hertz. The direction is the thing to keep straight, because the pure major third is 13.686 cents narrow and the pure minor third is 15.641 cents wide, and both errors push in the direction that makes a major third sound smaller and a minor third sound larger. The reason is that the pure minor third of six to five is built from the pure fifth, since 6 over 5 is 3 over 2 multiplied by 4 over 5, and it inherits the fifth's small width. The trap is 13.686, which is the figure for the major third, and it is easy to reach for because thirds are discussed together; the two figures are close in size but opposite in direction, and swapping them inverts the sound of a chord from slightly flat to slightly sharp.

questions.topic: Why a tuning cannot make every third and fifth exact
questions.learningObjective: explain why pure thirds and pure fifths are mutually exclusive
questions.stem: In 4/4, common time, in d major, a small ensemble is given a passage of open fifths and a second passage of major thirds in a major key, and it is asked to tune every one of them to the simplest ratio. Explain why no tuning can make all of them exact, and describe what the ensemble must give up.

answer.exemplar: No tuning can make every third and every fifth exact, and the obstruction is arithmetic rather than a matter of craft. A pure fifth is the ratio three to two, and a pure major third is five to four. If a note is fixed and both intervals are measured from it, then the note a twelfth above the first is three times the first note, because a fifth stacked on a fifth multiplies to nine over four, and a third above that twelfth is the pure third of five to four on top of that, giving nine over four times five to four, which is 45 over 16. But the same note reached by a different route, a pure major third below the fifth's top note, must be the pure third of four to five, giving two over three times four to five, which is eight over fifteen. Those two answers are not equal, because 45 over 16 is 2.8125 and eight over fifteen is 0.5333, and the ratio between the two routes is 531441 over 524288, which is the Pythagorean comma and measures 23.46 cents. The two routes disagree by that much, so one of the intervals on the route has to be stretched or squeezed, and there is no way to choose a value that satisfies all of them at once. The ensemble has to decide which interval to favour. Tuning so that the fifths are pure is the traditional choice, and it is why open fifths in a string ensemble or an unaccompanied choir sound so clear, but it forces the thirds on the other route to be noticeably sharp by 13.686 cents, and that sharpness is what a listener hears as the harshness of a badly tuned keyboard. Tuning so that the major thirds are pure instead makes every third in the key exact, which is the choice a fixed-pitch instrument such as an organ or a harpsichord tuned for one key has to make, and it forces the fifths on the other route 1.955 cents narrow. Equal temperament refuses to favour either: it splits the difference so that every key sounds the same, which leaves the fifth 1.955 cents wide, the major third 13.686 cents narrow, the minor third 15.641 cents wide, and the freedom to modulate freely. The wrong belief to avoid is that a better craftsman or a more expensive instrument removes the problem. The obstruction is the number system, so it survives any amount of skill and any budget.

questions.explanation: A pure fifth is three to two and a pure major third is five to four, and those two ratios are not consistent with each other, because going up a fifth and then a third gives a different answer from going up a third and then a fifth by the ratio 531441 over 524288, which is 23.46 cents. The consequence is that any fixed tuning must stretch some intervals to make others exact, and the choice of which to favour is a musical decision rather than a mathematical one: favour the fifths and the thirds go sharp, favour the thirds and the fifths go narrow.
questions.hint: Compare a fifth plus a third with a third plus a fifth, and find the ratio by which the two routes disagree.

questions.topic: The beat rate between two notes a semitone apart
questions.learningObjective: compute the beat rate produced by two close frequencies
questions.stem: Two players are a semitone apart: one holds the A4 at 440.00 hertz that the orchestra tuned to and the other holds the Bb4 a semitone above it, which equal temperament places at 466.16 hertz. How many beats per second does that pair produce, and why is a semitone too wide for beats to be heard as separate pulses?

options.text: The pair beats at 906.16 hertz, the sum of the two frequencies, since two pitches sounding together add their rates rather than subtract them
options.misconception: adds the frequencies instead of subtracting them

options.text: The pair beats at 26.16 hertz, the difference of 466.16 and 440.00, and beats are heard as separate pulses only below about 15 hertz, so 26.16 is heard as a continuous harshness instead
The pair beats at 2.00 hertz, since a semitone is 100 cents and each cent is worth 0.02 hertz at this height
options.misconception: converts cents straight into hertz

options.text: The pair beats at 26.16 hertz and the pulses are clearly audible, since any rate below the threshold of 30 hertz can be counted as separate beats
options.misconception: raises the beat-perception threshold without a basis

questions.explanation: Two tones close in frequency reinforce and cancel in turn, and the rate of that alternation is the difference between the two frequencies, never the sum. Here the difference is 466.16 minus 440.00, which is 26.16 hertz, so the pair would beat 26.16 times each second if the tones were slow enough for the rate to register as separate events. They are not, because a listener resolves beats as distinct pulses only from roughly 4 to 15 hertz; above about 15 hertz the two-tone complex is heard as a single sound with a harsh or gritty quality rather than as a pulsing, and at 26.16 hertz the result is a stable roughness. The consequence is practical, because a semitone is the smallest interval an orchestra has to play in tune, and so the 26.16 hertz figure does not tell a conductor anything about intonation. Intervals that matter for tuning are the unison, which beats at a few hertz for a difference of one or two cents, and the octave, where a two-cent error at 440 hertz gives 0.51 hertz. The trap in the first option is the sum, which is what two tones would produce if they were being multiplied in a circuit rather than superposed in air.
questions.hint: The beat rate is the difference of the two frequencies, and beats are only heard separately below about 15 hertz.

questions.topic: The beat rate between a pure and an equal-tempered third
questions.learningObjective: compute the beat rate of a mistuned third
questions.stem: A cellist holds a C4 at 261.63 hertz while a keyboard plays a C major chord tuned in equal temperament with A4 at 440 hertz, so its E4 sounds at 329.63 hertz. The cellist's third is 13.686 cents narrower than the keyboard's. How many beats per second does the pair produce?
questions.explanation: The beat rate is the difference of the two frequencies, so the pair beats at 329.63 minus the cellist's E, and the cellist's pure third above 261.6256 hertz is 261.6256 times five quarters, which is 327.032 hertz. The difference is 329.628 minus 327.032, which is 2.60 hertz, so the answer is 2.60 beats per second. A second route gets there from the cents: 13.686 cents is 0.11405 semitones, and 0.11405 times 100 cents per semitone is 13.686 cents, which at a height near 330 hertz corresponds to 2.60 hertz, since one cent at 330 hertz is worth about 1.91 hertz. The significance is the rate itself, because 2.60 hertz sits squarely inside the 4 to 15 hertz band where a listener hears separate beats, so this mistuning announces itself unmistakably as a wavering, whereas the 26.16 hertz of a semitone does not. That is why a mistuned third in an exposed texture is immediately obvious while a mistuned semitone can pass unnoticed, and it is the acoustic reason a cellist and a pianist playing the same chord cannot simply agree to be slightly out. The trap is 13.686, the cents figure, which is a measure of perceived pitch difference and not a rate.
questions.hint: Multiply the cellist's C4 by five quarters, then subtract that from the keyboard's equal-tempered E4.

questions.topic: The fundamental implied by a spectrum with no fundamental
questions.learningObjective: infer a missing fundamental by dividing a spectrum by whole numbers
questions.stem: A measured spectrum contains components at 300, 400, 500 and 600 hertz and no component below 300 hertz. What fundamental does the spectrum imply, and what is the connection between that pitch and the components the ear reports?

options.text: The implied fundamental is 100 hertz, since the four components are its 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th partials, and the ear reports a pitch of 100 hertz that is not itself present in the spectrum
The implied fundamental is 300 hertz, the lowest component present, and the ear must report the lowest component it receives because no other pitch can be inferred
options.misconception: assumes the lowest measured component must be the fundamental

options.text: The implied fundamental is 200 hertz, since 300 and 500 are its third and fifth partials and the middle components fit a series rooted there
options.misconception: fits a partial series that leaves gaps in the component list

options.text: The implied fundamental is 100 hertz, and the ear reports 200 hertz instead, because the ear always reports a pitch one octave above the series root
options.misconception: supposes the auditory system shifts the implied pitch up an octave

questions.explanation: A harmonic series has every partial at a whole-number multiple of its fundamental, so the fundamental is found by dividing the components by whole numbers and looking for the smallest number that leaves no gaps. Dividing 300, 400, 500 and 600 hertz by 100 gives 3, 4, 5 and 6, four consecutive whole numbers, and dividing them by any larger candidate leaves a gap: by 200 they give 1.5, 2, 2.5 and 3, which is not a harmonic series. So the root is 100 hertz. What makes the effect famous is the discrepancy between what is measured and what is heard, because no component at 100 hertz exists in the spectrum, yet a listener pressing the lowest tone of a chord on a piano while hearing the recording reports a pitch at 100 hertz, below everything in the signal. The auditory system recovers the missing term by a pattern it has evolved for exactly this situation, which is also why a telephone reproduces the voice and loses the music: a band-limited signal carries no information about a fundamental below its own lowest component. The trap in the third option is a real and separate phenomenon, the octave ambiguity of complex tones, but it applies when the spectrum is genuinely ambiguous, and here the series is unambiguous.
questions.hint: Divide the components by 100 and by 200 and see which gives consecutive whole numbers with no gaps.

questions.topic: The harmonic a stopped cylindrical pipe sounds at its fifth harmonic
questions.learningObjective: compute the frequency of a specific harmonic of a stopped pipe
questions.stem: A clarinet in B flat is given a written C4 quarter note in 4/4, common time, in concert f major, and sounds Bb3 at 233.08 hertz with A4 at 440 hertz. A clarinet is a stopped cylindrical pipe, so it sounds only the odd harmonics, one, three, five and seven. What is the frequency in hertz of the fifth harmonic it sounds, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: The fifth harmonic is five times the fundamental, so 233.0819 hertz times five is 1165.41 hertz, which is the answer. The reason a clarinet sounds only the odd harmonics is physical and worth stating, because it is the same reason its tone is hollow: the pipe is stopped at the mouthpiece end, so the air column can only fit an odd number of quarter wavelengths, and a stopped column of length L sounds a fundamental of v over four L while an open column of the same length sounds v over two L, one octave lower. The first four partials of a clarinet are therefore the 1st, the 3rd, the 5th and the 7th, at 233.08, 699.25, 1165.41 and 1631.57 hertz, and the missing even partials are what make the instrument sound hollow rather than reedy, so the flute and the oboe, which are open at both ends and have all their partials, are brighter. A second route confirms the figure: five is a whole number of the fundamental, and 1165.41 divided by 233.08 is exactly 5. The trap is 699.25, which is the third harmonic and the one a beginner reaches for, since the two are the first and second odd numbers and are easily transposed.
questions.hint: Five times 233.08 hertz, because a clarinet sounds only odd harmonics and the fifth is the third of them.

questions.topic: A stretched octave at the top of a piano keyboard
questions.learningObjective: compute the size of a stretched octave in cents
questions.stem: A piano tuner strikes the A4 at the standard 440.00 hertz and then the A5 a little above it at 444.00 hertz, having stretched that octave so the top of the keyboard matches the instrument's own partials. How many cents wide is that stretched octave, against the 1200.0 cents of an exact octave?
questions.explanation: The width of a ratio in cents is 1200 x log2 of the ratio, and the ratio here is 444.00 over 440.00, which is 1.0090909, so the octave measures 1200 x log2 of 1.0090909, which is 15.67 cents. Subtracting from the exact 1200.0 is not needed, because the exact octave is already the 1200 in the formula. A second route confirms the figure from the beat rate: the two tones differ by 4.00 hertz, and at a height near 440 hertz one cent is worth about 2.54 hertz, so 4.00 hertz is 1.57 cents at A4, and because the error is spread across an octave the total stretch is about ten times that at the top, which lands in the same region as 15.67 cents. The practice being measured is real, since a piano's upper strings are short and their stiffness raises their partials, so the 2nd, 3rd and 4th partials sit progressively higher than a harmonic series built on the fundamental would predict, and a tuner matches the beats between the upper partials instead of the strings' fundamental lengths. The upper octaves of a concert grand are typically a few cents wide, and the trap is 0, which would be true only of an instrument with no stiffness at all.
questions.hint: Use 1200 times the base 2 logarithm of 444 divided by 440.

questions.topic: A level difference stated in decibels
questions.learningObjective: convert a decibel level difference into an intensity ratio
questions.stem: A recording of a movement in 4/4, common time, in e minor has its quietest passage measured at 40 decibels and its loudest at 100 decibels on the same sound level meter. What is the level difference in decibels, and how many times greater is the intensity of the loudest passage than of the quietest?
questions.explanation: The level difference is 100 minus 40, which is 60 decibels, and the intensity ratio follows from the definition of the decibel scale, where a difference of 10 decibels means ten times the intensity, so a difference of 60 decibels is 10 to the 6th power, which is 1000000. A check by repeated doubling confirms the scale's structure: every 3 decibels doubles the intensity, so 60 decibels is 20 doublings, and 2 to the 20th power is 1048576, which rounds to about 1000000, the small difference being that 3.01 rather than 3 decibels is the exact doubling interval. The practical significance is that the number makes clear how much of a recording's dynamic range is being used, since a 60 decibel span is wide enough to convey a whole crescendo and narrow enough that the quietest material is not swamped, and the human threshold of audibility is usually placed 40 to 50 decibels below the level of ordinary speech. The trap is 1000, which is what a 30 decibel difference gives and which is a far more usual figure, or 100, which is what a 20 decibel difference gives.
questions.hint: Subtract the levels, then use the fact that 10 decibels is a factor of ten in intensity.

options.text: They are four independent equal-tempered pitches, B3, F#4, B4 and D#5, which are the notes of a B major triad with an added octave rather than the partials of a single note
options.misconception: reads a single note as a four-note chord

options.text: They are the 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th partials of a fundamental of 164.63 hertz, since 246.94 is 1.5 times 164.63 and a series may begin at three halves

The trap in the first option is the useful one, since the nearest equal-tempered names do form a recognisable chord and it takes the division to show that a single note produced them.

questions.topic: The frequency of a fretted note on a guitar string
questions.learningObjective: compute the frequency reached by raising a string by a stated number of semitones
questions.stem: A guitarist in 4/4, common time, in d major frets the open A string of a guitar in standard tuning, whose open pitch is A2 at 110.00 hertz, up to the 7th fret. Taking A4 at 440 hertz in equal temperament, what is the frequency in hertz of that fretted note, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: A fretted guitar gives one semitone per fret, so the 7th fret is seven semitones above A2, and the note number of A2 is 45, so seven semitones lands on 52. Note number 52 is E3, which is a perfect fifth above A2, and its frequency is 440 x 2 to the power of (52 - 69) divided by 12, which is 440 x 2 to the power of -17 divided by 12, a factor of 0.374655, and the product is 164.81 hertz. A second route confirms it: A2 is 110.00 hertz, and seven semitones is a perfect fifth, a factor of 2 to the power of 7 divided by 12, which is 1.498307, and 110.00 times 1.498307 is 164.81. The reason the semitone count is exactly one per fret is geometric, since a fret is placed at the point along the string where the remaining length gives the required frequency, and equal temperament's constant ratio of 2 to the 1 divided by 12 means each fret shortens the string by the same proportion. Two checks on the notation close the item: E3 is a diatonic member of d major, so no accidental is needed, and the 12th fret of any string repeats its open pitch one octave up, which is the landmark that guitarists actually use. The traps are 146.83, which is the 5th fret, and 185.00, which is the 9th fret.
questions.hint: Seven semitones above A2 is E3, so use note number 52 in the equal-temperament formula.

questions.topic: The twelfth fret of a guitar string
questions.learningObjective: identify the pitch at the twelfth fret of a string
questions.stem: A guitarist in 4/4, common time, in e major frets the open low E string of a guitar in standard tuning, whose open pitch is E2, up to the 12th fret. What is the pitch at that fret, and why is the 12th fret such a useful landmark?

options.text: The 12th fret is E4, two octaves above the open E2, because twelve frets raise the pitch by a whole tone each, and a whole tone is an octave
options.misconception: counts twelve whole tones as one octave

options.text: The 12th fret is B2, a perfect fifth above the open E2, because twelve frets on a six-string guitar count from the nut to the eleventh and the last one is the fifth
options.misconception: miscounts the frets between the nut and the octave

options.text: The 12th fret is E3, a perfect octave above the open E2, because twelve semitones make one octave, and the fret is the point where the string's length is exactly half, which is also the midpoint harmonic
The 12th fret is C4, two octaves and a whole tone above the open E2, because each fret adds a whole tone and twelve whole tones reach two octaves
options.misconception: treats a fret as a whole tone and reaches two octaves

questions.explanation: Twelve semitones is one octave, so the 12th fret of the open E2 string sounds E3, and the intermediate frets check the count: the 3rd fret is G2, a minor third up, and the 7th fret is B2, a perfect fifth up, so twelve semitones completes the octave from E2 to E3. The landmark is worth memorising for a geometric reason as well as a numerical one, since a fret is placed where the vibrating length of the string produces the required frequency, and because a string's pitch is inversely proportional to its vibrating length the 12th fret lands at exactly half the nut-to-bridge distance. Halving the length doubles the frequency, which is precisely what an octave is, and it is also why lightly touching an open string at its midpoint produces the same pitch as the 12th fret. That single fact ties the fretboard to the harmonic series, and it is why the 12th fret and the octave harmonic are the same pitch. The trap in the third option miscounts what a fret does, since one fret is a semitone and twelve frets are an octave and not two.
questions.hint: Twelve semitones is one octave, and the 12th fret stops the string at half its length.

questions.topic: The interval between two fret positions
questions.learningObjective: compute the interval between two fretted notes on a string
questions.stem: In 4/4, common time, in g major, a guitarist moves from the 5th fret of the open A string, which sounds D3, to the 7th fret of the same string, which sounds E3. How many semitones separate the two positions, and what is the interval between D3 and E3?
questions.explanation: The two frets differ by 7 minus 5, which is 2, and each fret is one semitone, so the two notes are 2 semitones apart. The name follows from the letters: D3 to E3 spans the two letter names D and E, so it is a second, and 2 semitones makes that a major second, a whole tone. A second route confirms it: the note numbers are 50 and 52, and 52 minus 50 is 2. The reason the fret count and the semitone count always agree is that the fret spacing is exponential rather than even, since each fret sits at a fixed fraction of the distance from the bridge, so the frets get closer together as they approach the 12th and closer together still beyond it. An even spacing would produce unequal semitones, and the exponential spacing is what makes every fret an exact equal-tempered semitone. The check that the passage is in g major is easy, because D3 and E3 are both members of g major, which has one sharp, so neither needs an accidental. The trap is 1, which would be the case if the fret spacing were even, and 12, which is what a difference of twelve fret numbers would give.
questions.hint: Count the fret difference, because one fret is one semitone, then name the two pitches.

questions.topic: The sounding pitch of an electric bass note
questions.learningObjective: convert a written electric bass pitch into a sounding pitch
questions.stem: An electric bass part in 4/4, common time, in a minor, is written in the bass clef a quarter note on C4 followed by a half note on E3, which together fill the bar. What does the bass actually sound, and how does that compare with the sounding pitch of a double bass on the same written notes?

options.text: The electric bass sounds C4 and then E3 as written, because a bass clef already indicates the low register and needs no octave correction
options.misconception: believes a bass clef implies an octave displacement

options.text: The electric bass sounds C3 and then E2, an octave below the written notes, and a double bass written the same notes would sound the same C3 and E2 because both instruments are written an octave above sounding
The electric bass sounds C5 and then E4, an octave above written, because a four-string bass is tuned to the same notes as a guitar
options.misconception: gives the bass the guitar octave direction

options.text: The electric bass sounds C2 and then E1, two octaves below written, because every bass instrument carries two octave displacements at once
options.misconception: applies two octave displacements to the same part

questions.explanation: The electric bass is notated an octave above the pitch it produces, the same convention the double bass follows, so a written C4 sounds C3 and a written E3 sounds E2. The reason is the same physical constraint in both cases: a bass's lowest string is around a metre long, so a family of much shorter strings would be needed to reach the higher notes, and writing the part up lets the player use the strings that exist. The comparison in the question is the useful part, because a double bass and an electric bass on the same written note produce the same sounding pitch, which is what lets a bass line be notated identically for the two and only the timbre changes. The written pitches' place in the bar is worth confirming: a quarter note is 1 beat and a half note is 2, and 1 plus 2 is 3, which does not fill a 4/4 bar, so the bar as described is short by one beat. The trap in the first option is the confusion between a clef and a transposition: a clef moves a note on the page and a transposition moves its pitch, and only the transposition changes what sounds.
questions.hint: Both basses are written an octave above sounding, so the written C4 and E3 become C3 and E2.

questions.topic: A natural harmonic at the midpoint of a string
questions.learningObjective: name the pitch a midpoint natural harmonic produces
questions.stem: A violinist in 4/4, common time, in d major lightly touches the G string of the violin exactly at its midpoint with one finger and bows the string. The open G string sounds G3 at 196.00 hertz with A4 at 440 hertz. What pitch does the touched note sound, and what physical fact produces it?

options.text: The touched note sounds G4 at 392.00 hertz, a perfect octave above G3, because touching at the midpoint suppresses every partial that does not fit a whole number of equal loops and leaves the 2nd partial alone
The touched note sounds G3 at 196.00 hertz, the same pitch as the open string, because a light touch does not change the string tension
options.misconception: believes a light touch cannot change the pitch

options.text: The touched note sounds D4, a perfect fifth above the open G3, because touching at the midpoint leaves the 3rd partial and removes the 2nd
options.misconception: names the 3rd partial instead of the 2nd for a midpoint touch

options.text: The touched note sounds G5, two octaves above the open G3, because a midpoint touch doubles the frequency twice rather than once
options.misconception: double counts the doubling

questions.explanation: Touching a string at a point does not shorten it, so the tension and the mass per unit length are unchanged; what the touch does is mark a node, and any partial that would have a wave crossing that point is suppressed, leaving only the partials with a node there. At the midpoint the surviving partials are the even ones, because a partial of order n has n loops along the string and therefore n minus 1 internal nodes, so it has a node at the midpoint only when n is even. The lowest survivor is therefore the 2nd partial, and a 2nd partial is a perfect octave above the fundamental, which is why the midpoint harmonic on any string sounds an octave up rather than at the open pitch. The frequency is exactly double, so G3 at 196.00 hertz becomes G4 at 392.00 hertz. The check against the fretboard is the same fact seen another way, since the 12th fret stops the string at half its length, and a string stopped at half its length vibrates in two loops. The trap in the second option is the third partial, which is what a touch one third of the way along produces.
questions.hint: A midpoint touch leaves only the even partials, and the lowest even partial is the 2nd, which is an octave up.
