questions.topic: The frequency of a third-position natural harmonic on a string
questions.learningObjective: compute the frequency of a natural harmonic a twelfth above a string
questions.stem: A cellist in 4/4, common time, in g major bows the D string of the cello, whose open pitch is D3 at 146.83 hertz, touching it lightly at one third of its length. Taking A4 at 440 hertz in equal temperament, what is the frequency in hertz of that natural harmonic, to two decimal places, and what is the nearest equal-tempered note?
questions.explanation: A touch at one third of a string's length leaves the partials whose order is a multiple of three, so the lowest survivor is the 3rd partial, and the 3rd partial is three times the fundamental. Multiplying, 3 times 146.83 hertz is 440.50 hertz, which is the answer. The nearest equal-tempered note is A4 at 440.00 hertz, and the partial sits 2.0 cents above it, which is the small width that makes a string's fifths nearly pure, and the interval above the open string is a perfect twelfth, since D3 up to A4 is 19 semitones. Two independent routes confirm the figure: the formula route gives A4's neighbours directly, since 19 semitones above D3 is A4 and the 3rd partial is a twelfth above the fundamental, and the ratio route notes that 3 divided by 2 is one and a half, so the 3rd partial is one and a half times the 2nd partial, and the 2nd partial of the D string is 293.66 hertz while 293.66 times one and a half is 440.50. The notation check is that A4 is a member of g major, which has one sharp, so no accidental is needed. The traps are 293.66, which is the octave and therefore the midpoint harmonic rather than the third-position one, and 146.83, which is the open string itself.
questions.hint: A touch one third along leaves the 3rd partial, which is three times the fundamental, so 3 times 146.83 hertz.

questions.topic: The speaking length of a string for a stated pitch
questions.learningObjective: compute a string length from its pitch and wave speed
questions.stem: A bowed string sounds a fundamental of A3, which is 220.00 hertz in equal temperament with A4 at 440 hertz, and the waves travel along the string at 330 metres per second. What is the length in metres of the string section that vibrates, to three decimal places?
questions.explanation: A string fixed at both ends fits a whole number of half-wavelengths along its length, so the fundamental's wavelength is twice the speaking length, and the length is the wave speed divided by twice the frequency. That gives 330 divided by 2 times 220.00, which is 330 divided by 440.00, and the result is 0.750 metres. Two independent routes agree. The formula route from the physics is length = speed over 2 f, and the note-number route is the same division, since A3 is 220.00 hertz and half its wavelength is 330 over 440.00 metres. A check by doubling gives the same scale one octave up: A4 at 440.00 hertz needs 0.375 metres, and a string half as long sounds an octave higher, which is the relation that underlies the 12th fret and the octave harmonic alike. The practical reading is that a bass string sounding E2 at 82.41 hertz would need 2.002 metres by the same formula, which is why a double bass's longest string is close to two metres, and the 0.750 metres here is a cello-scale length. The trap is 1.500, which is the full wavelength rather than half of it, and 0.150, which forgets the factor of two in the other direction.
questions.hint: The length is the wave speed divided by twice the frequency, since a string fits half a wavelength at its fundamental.

questions.topic: The interval between two timpani drums
questions.learningObjective: name the interval between two stated timpani pitches
questions.stem: A timpanist tunes the two drums of a pair in 4/4, common time, in d minor to D3 and to A2. What interval separates the two drums, counted from the higher drum down to the lower, and how many semitones is it?

options.text: The interval is a perfect fifth, seven semitones, counted from D3 down to A2, since a fifth is the standard span of a timpani pair
options.misconception: names a fifth because pairs are thought to span a fifth

options.text: The interval is a major third, four semitones, counted from D3 down to A2, since the letters D, C, B and A give three steps and therefore a third
options.misconception: miscounts the letter names in the descending span

options.text: The interval is a minor third, three semitones, counted from D3 down to A2, since the note numbers of D3 and A2 differ by three
options.misconception: reads a five-semitone gap as three semitones

options.text: The interval is a perfect fourth, five semitones, counted from D3 down to A2, since the letters D, C, B and A give four steps and the semitone count of five makes it perfect

questions.explanation: Two things have to be checked, the letters and the semitones, and they have to agree. Counting down from D3 toward A2 the letters are D, C, B, A, which is four letter names and therefore a fourth, and the semitone count is D3 at 50 minus A2 at 45, which is 5, and a fourth of 5 semitones is perfect. Counted the other way, from A2 up to D3, the interval is still a perfect fourth, since a fourth is its own inversion and the two drums keep the same five-semitone span whichever note is named first. The practical context is the standard set of timpani pitches, which on a full set are spaced so that each drum lies a fifth from the next, and a two-drum pair is often taken as a fifth apart, D3 with A3, precisely so that a player can reach either from the other with one stroke; this pair, D3 with A2, is therefore a deliberately close-spaced fourth, chosen so that two notes a fifth apart are available in the same register. The trap in the first option is the useful one, since a fifth apart is the normal choice and a reader who assumes the normal case will misname a pair that is not normal.
questions.hint: Count the letters D, C, B and A for the number, and subtract the note numbers for the semitones.

questions.topic: A timpani drum retuned by a pedal movement
questions.learningObjective: name the interval a timpani pedal move produces
questions.stem: A timpanist is playing a drum tuned to A2 in 4/4, common time, in d minor and needs a move to the lowered note a semitone below. What is the resulting pitch, what interval has the drum been moved by, and what has physically changed on the drum head?

options.text: The new pitch is A#2, the drum has been raised by a minor second of one semitone, and the change is made by tightening the head through the pedal
options.misconception: raises the pitch when lowering it and mislabels the direction

options.text: The new pitch is Ab2, the drum has been lowered by a whole tone of two semitones, and the change is made by slackening the tension of the head through the pedal
options.misconception: turns a semitone move into a whole tone

options.text: The new pitch is G#2, the drum has been lowered by a minor second of one semitone, and the change is made by slackening the tension of the head through the pedal, which lowers the pitch of every partial it produces
The new pitch is G2, the drum has been lowered by a major third of four semitones, and the change is made by moving the drum closer to the player's ear
options.misconception: gives the timpani a chromatic rather than a mechanical change

questions.explanation: A pedal timpani changes pitch by altering the tension of the head, and a head under less tension vibrates more slowly, so the pitch falls. Lowering A2 by one semitone gives a pitch one semitone below A2, and the correct spelling of that pitch is G#2 rather than Ab2, because a lowered note keeps its letter and takes a flat, and a key signature is not involved here since the drum is retuned rather than respelled. The interval from the original A2 down to the new G#2 is a minor second, and a minor second is one semitone. The check is the note numbers: A2 is 45 and G#2 is 44, a difference of 1. What changes physically is not the pitch of one note but the whole series the drum produces, since tension scales every partial at once, so a drum tuned to A2 and lowered to G#2 gives a series rooted on G#2, and its 2nd partial falls from A3 to G#3 with it. That is the practical reason a timpanist thinks in terms of a whole set of available pitches and not one drum at a time. The trap in the second option is the whole tone, which is the nearest other pedal move and the one a beginner reaches for because a key signature changes by whole steps.
questions.hint: Lowering a note by a semitone keeps the letter and adds a sharp, and the pedal changes head tension.

questions.topic: The octave displacement of tuned percussion bars
questions.learningObjective: compare the sounding pitches of two tuned percussion instruments
questions.stem: A marimba and a xylophone play in the same bar in 4/4, common time, in c major, and both parts are written a quarter note on C4. The marimba is notated at sounding pitch and the xylophone is notated an octave below sounding. What do the two instruments actually produce, and what interval separates them?

options.text: Both instruments sound C4, since the two parts are written identically and identical notation must give identical sound
options.misconception: assumes identical notation implies identical sounding pitch

options.text: The marimba sounds C4 and the xylophone sounds C5, and the two are a perfect octave apart, twelve semitones, because the xylophone's part is written an octave below the pitch its bars produce
The marimba sounds C5 and the xylophone sounds C4, and the two are a perfect octave apart, because the marimba's higher bars take the part up an octave
options.misconception: reverses which instrument is displaced

options.text: The marimba sounds C4 and the xylophone sounds C3, and the two are a perfect octave apart, because the xylophone is written an octave below sounding and the reading is inverted
options.misconception: reads an octave-below-written rule as an octave-down shift

questions.explanation: The xylophone's bars are short and hard, so their pitches sit an octave above where a part for them is written, and the convention is that the written note is the lower of the two. A written C4 therefore means the bar that sounds C5, while the marimba's bar is notated at the pitch it sounds, so its written C4 sounds C4. The interval between the two sounding pitches is a perfect octave, which is 12 semitones, and the check is the note numbers: the marimba's C4 is 60 and the xylophone's C5 is 72, and 72 minus 60 is 12. The practical consequence is that an orchestral part for marimba and xylophone doubles at the octave, which is the standard way to give the two a shared melodic line while keeping the bright attack of the xylophone audible above the marimba's wood. The trap in the third option is a real and common reading error, because "written an octave below sounding" is easy to reverse into "sounds an octave below written", and the two statements are opposites.
questions.hint: An instrument notated an octave below sounding produces the pitch an octave above its written note.

questions.topic: The distance between the lowest strings of a cello and a viola
questions.learningObjective: compute the interval between two stated lowest string pitches
questions.stem: A viola's lowest string is tuned to C3 and a cello's lowest string to C2, both in 4/4, common time, in a passage in c major. How many semitones separate the viola's lowest open string from the cello's lowest open string, and what interval is that?
questions.explanation: The two pitches are an octave apart, and an octave is 12 semitones, so the answer is 12. The arithmetic: C3 has note number 48 and C2 has note number 36, and 48 minus 36 is 12. The letter count agrees, since the two notes carry the same letter and an octave is the only interval that repeats a letter name, so a count of D, C, B, A, G, F, E, D, C gives eight steps and therefore an octave. The check against the key is straightforward, because both C2 and C3 are the tonic of c major in different octaves, so a passage can use either without an accidental. The practical reason this is worth knowing is the notation consequence: the cello's bass clef reaches down to C2 on the ledger line below the staff, while the viola's alto clef puts C3 on the bottom line of its staff, so a cellist and a violist reading the same sounding note are reading it in very different places on the page. The trap is 19, which is the distance from a cello's C2 up to a violin's lowest G3 and is a twelfth rather than an octave.
questions.hint: C2 and C3 are the same letter name, so the interval is an octave, and an octave is 12 semitones.

questions.topic: The lowest string of the viola against that of the violin
questions.learningObjective: name the interval between two orchestral string instruments lowest strings
questions.stem: A viola's lowest string is C3 and a violin's lowest string is G3, both tuned before a rehearsal in 4/4, common time, of a piece in g major. What interval lies between the two lowest strings, and which of the two instruments can reach the lower one?

options.text: The interval is a perfect fifth, seven semitones, from C3 up to G3, and only the viola can reach C3, since G3 is already the bottom of the violin's range and a fifth below it lies out of reach
The interval is a perfect fourth, five semitones, from C3 up to G3, since the letters C, D, E, F and G give five steps and therefore a fourth
options.misconception: miscounts the letter names as a fourth

options.text: The interval is a perfect fifth, seven semitones, from C3 up to G3, and both instruments can reach C3, since the violin shares the viola's tuning at the bottom of its range
options.misconception: believes a violin reaches down to a viola's lowest string

options.text: The interval is an octave, twelve semitones, from C3 up to G3, since the two instruments are tuned a doubling apart at their lowest strings
options.misconception: calls a fifth an octave

questions.explanation: The semitone count is decisive: C3 has note number 48 and G3 has note number 55, and 55 minus 48 is 7. The letter count agrees, since C, D, E, F and G is five letter names and therefore a fifth, and a fifth of 7 semitones is perfect. So the viola's bottom string sits a perfect fifth below the violin's, and because a violin's lowest open string is its own floor, the viola's lowest note is out of the violin's range entirely, which is why violin parts are written an octave higher in a mixed string texture. The key check is that both pitches are members of g major, which has one sharp, so a tuning check needs no accidental on either string. The two clefs show the same fact in notation: the violin's C3 would sit well below its treble staff, on three ledger lines, while the viola reads C3 on the bottom line of the alto staff with no ledger line at all. The trap in the third option is a doubling that does not exist, and the trap in the second is the assumption that neighbouring instruments in a section share their bottom strings.
questions.hint: Subtract the note numbers, C3 at 48 and G3 at 55, and then count the letters C through G.

questions.topic: Tracing the rule that converts a fret number to a pitch
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that adds a fret count to a string note number
questions.stem: Trace the rule fretted(open, n), which returns the note number of a fretted note on a string: fretted(open, n) = return note(open) + n, where note() is the MIDI number of the pitch name and n is the fret number. Apply it to a bar in 4/4, common time, in g major, on a guitar in standard tuning whose open strings are E2, A2, D3, G3 and B3, using a written quarter note at the 3rd fret of the A string, a quarter note at the 7th fret of the D string and a half note at the 7th fret of the G string. What three note names does the rule return?

options.text: A3, D4 and G4, since the rule adds the fret number to the note number of the next higher string in the list rather than to the string named
options.misconception: shifts each note up to the next string before adding the fret

options.text: C3, A3 and D4 read as C4, A4 and D5, since the rule returns a note number and the caller must add an octave to reach the guitar octave
options.misconception: adds an extra octave to the returned note numbers

options.text: F#2, G#2 and A2, since the rule subtracts the fret number from the open string, because a fret shortens the string
options.misconception: subtracts the fret count instead of adding it

options.text: C3, A3 and D4, since note(A2) is 45 and 45 plus 3 is 48, note(D3) is 50 and 50 plus 7 is 57, and note(G3) is 55 and 55 plus 7 is 62

questions.explanation: Three additions and three conversions, and the string note numbers have to be right first. A2 is 45, D3 is 50 and G3 is 55 in standard tuning, and adding the fret numbers 3, 7 and 7 gives 48, 57 and 62. Converting back, 48 is C3, 57 is A3 and 62 is D4. The key check confirms the trace: g major has one sharp, and C3, A3 and D4 are all members of g major, so none of the three needs an accidental, which is what a composer writing a diatonic guitar line in g major would expect. The relation being used is the geometric one, since each fret raises the pitch by exactly one semitone, so the rule is addition of a count, and the fact that the frets get physically closer together as they climb does not change the pitch step. The traps in the second and third options are the two directions a beginner gets wrong, and both are worth naming precisely: the guitar's written range is the sounding range, so nothing needs an octave added, and a fret raises rather than lowers the pitch, because pressing a string shortens the vibrating length and shorter means faster and higher.
questions.hint: Convert the three open strings to note numbers, add the fret numbers, then convert the results back to pitch names.

questions.topic: Tracing the rule that reads a partial number
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that multiplies a fundamental by a partial number
questions.stem: Trace the rule partial(f0, n), which returns the frequency in hertz of the nth partial of a string: partial(f0, n) = return n * f0. Apply it with f0 = 261.63, the frequency of a C4, to the partials 2, 3, 5 and 7. Give the four frequencies, and name the pitch nearest to each in equal temperament with A4 at 440 hertz.

options.text: 261.63, 392.45, 654.08 and 784.88 hertz, which are nearest to C4, G4, E5 and G5, since the rule divides the fundamental by the partial number
options.misconception: divides by the partial number instead of multiplying

options.text: 523.25, 784.88, 1308.13 and 1831.38 hertz, which are nearest to C5, G5, E6 and A6, since the 7th partial is a major sixth above the 6th
options.misconception: names the 7th partial by a rule that fits sixths, not sevenths

options.text: 523.25, 784.88, 1308.13 and 1831.38 hertz, which are nearest to C5, G5, E6 and the A sharp 6 that equal temperament names A#6 and that is enharmonically Bb6, since each is the fundamental multiplied by its partial number
261.63, 523.25, 784.88 and 1046.50 hertz, which are nearest to C4, C5, G5 and C6, since the rule returns the frequency of the interval above the fundamental
options.misconception: returns the spacing between partials rather than the partials themselves

questions.explanation: The rule is a multiplication, so the four products are 2 times 261.63, which is 523.25, 3 times 261.63, which is 784.88, 5 times 261.63, which is 1308.13, and 7 times 261.63, which is 1831.38. Naming each in equal temperament means finding the note number whose frequency is nearest, and those are 72, 79, 89 and 94, which are C5, G5, E6 and Bb6. The shape of the answer is worth noticing: the partials 2, 3 and 5 give C5, G5 and E6, which are the root, fifth and third of a C major triad spread over two octaves, and the 7th partial would supply the Bb that completes a dominant seventh built on that root. That is the harmonic reason a single note implies a dominant seventh chord built on itself, and it is why the 7th partial's nearest note, Bb6, is 31.2 cents flat of the equal-tempered Bb. The trap in the first option divides rather than multiplies, which would produce a subharmonic series, and subharmonics are a real thing but they are not what this rule does. The trap in the second option gets the arithmetic right and the naming wrong, since the 7th partial of a C is a seventh above the octave, not a sixth.
questions.hint: Multiply the fundamental by each partial number, then find the nearest equal-tempered note to each product.

questions.topic: Reading a table of instrument transpositions
questions.learningObjective: extract the sounding pitch of each row of a transposition table
questions.stem: A table of an orchestra's transpositions lists six rows, each with a written C4 and the instrument's name: the flute, the oboe, the clarinet in B flat, the horn in F, the english horn in F and the piccolo. In 4/4, common time, in f major, what is each row's sounding pitch, and which rows sound lower than written?

options.text: The six sounding pitches are C4, C4, Bb3, F3, F3 and C3, and the three rows that sound lower are the clarinet, the horn and the english horn
options.misconception: places the piccolo an octave below written instead of above

options.text: The six sounding pitches are C4, C4, Bb3, F3, F3 and C5, and the three rows that sound lower than written are the B flat clarinet at Bb3, the horn in F at F3 and the english horn in F at F3
The six sounding pitches are all C4, and no row sounds lower, because the table lists a written C4 for every instrument and the written pitch is the sounding pitch
options.misconception: reads the written column as if it were the sounding column

options.text: The six sounding pitches are C4, C4, D4, G3, G3 and C5, and the horn rows sound higher than written, because a horn in F sounds the pitch named after it
options.misconception: reads the instrument name as the sounding pitch rather than as the pitch for a written C

questions.explanation: The rule that resolves the whole table is the meaning of the letter in a transposing instrument's name: it is the pitch the instrument produces when a written C4 appears, and every other written note follows the same relation. So a flute in C and an oboe, both in C, produce C4 from a written C4 and sit at concert pitch. A clarinet in B flat produces Bb3, a whole tone lower. A horn in F and an english horn in F both produce F3, a perfect fifth lower, which is also why the two rows are identical in the table even though the english horn is a woodwind and the horn a brass. A piccolo produces C5, an octave higher. Reading down the list gives C4, C4, Bb3, F3, F3 and C5, and the three that are lower than the written C4 are the clarinet and the two F instruments. The check against the key is that all six sounding pitches belong to f major, which has one flat, since Bb3 and F3 are members of f major and the others are the tonic, so a table that produced an accidental in the sounding column would be signalling an error. The trap in the third option is the single most common misreading of the convention, treating the name's letter as the sounding pitch for the written note rather than as the sounding pitch for a written C4.
questions.hint: The letter in the name is the pitch produced for a written C4, and every other written note shifts by the same amount.

questions.topic: Ordering written pitches by their sounding pitches
questions.learningObjective: rank written notes from different transposing parts by sounding pitch
questions.stem: Four players in 4/4, common time, in f major are each given the same written pitch, a written C5 half note. The players are a horn in F, a clarinet in B flat, an oboe and a trumpet in D. Put the four players in order from the one whose C5 sounds lowest to the one whose C5 sounds highest.

options.text: The horn in F, then the clarinet in B flat, then the oboe, then the trumpet in D, since the sounding pitches are F4, Bb4, C5 and D5 in that order of height
The trumpet in D, then the oboe, then the clarinet in B flat, then the horn in F, since the trumpet in D sounds highest and the ranking is asked from the highest down
options.misconception: ranks from highest to lowest instead of lowest to highest

options.text: The horn in F, then the clarinet in B flat, then the trumpet in D, then the oboe, since a D instrument is a transposing instrument and therefore ranks below a non-transposing one
options.misconception: ranks by whether an instrument transposes rather than by sounding pitch

options.text: The clarinet in B flat, then the horn in F, then the oboe, then the trumpet in D, since a B flat instrument falls a tone and an F instrument falls a fifth, so the tone is the larger fall
options.misconception: reverses the sizes of the tone and the fifth

questions.explanation: Each written C5 has to be converted before the four can be compared, and the conversions are these. The horn in F drops a perfect fifth, so its written C5 sounds F4. The clarinet in B flat drops a whole tone, so its written C5 sounds Bb4. The oboe does not transpose, so its written C5 sounds C5. The trumpet in D rises a whole tone, so its written C5 sounds D5. With the note numbers in hand the ranking is immediate: F4 is 65, Bb4 is 70, C5 is 72 and D5 is 74, and those increase in that order. The key check confirms every row, since all four sounding pitches are members of f major, which has one flat, and Bb4 in particular needs no accidental there. The pedagogical point is that the ranking has nothing to do with how conspicuous the transposition is: a fifth and a tone are both small, and the only reliable method is to convert each row and then compare numbers. The trap in the fourth option is the arithmetic of the two lower rows, since a fifth of 7 semitones is larger than a tone of 2 and therefore places the horn lower, not higher.
questions.hint: Convert each written C5 to its sounding pitch, then compare the four note numbers.

questions.topic: The pedal tones of a brass instrument
questions.learningObjective: derive the written pedal tones of a horn from its harmonic series
questions.stem: A brass instrument can sound only the partials of its own tube, and the lowest of them are called its pedal tones. On a horn in F, in 4/4, common time, in f major, a written C4 sounds the fundamental F3. Which four written notes produce the first four partials above that fundamental, F3, F4, C5 and F5?

options.text: The four written notes are F3, F4, C5 and F5, since the pedal tones are the partials themselves and the part is written at the pitches the instrument produces
options.misconception: writes the sounding pitches into a transposing part

options.text: The four written notes are C4, F4, G4 and C5, since a perfect fifth below C4 is F3, a fifth below F4 is Bb3, and the pedal tones rise in whole tones
options.misconception: applies the fifth transposition in the wrong direction for the higher partials

options.text: The four written notes are C4, C5, E5 and G5, since the partials of a tube are an octave, a twelfth, a seventeenth and a nineteenth and those map onto C, C, E and G
options.misconception: names partial numbers as intervals without converting to written notes

options.text: The four written notes are C4, C5, G5 and C6, since every written note of a horn in F sounds a perfect fifth below itself, and C4 sounds F3, C5 sounds F4, G5 sounds C5 and C6 sounds F5

questions.explanation: The conversion is the same one that governs the whole part: a horn in F sounds a perfect fifth below whatever is written, so each sounding pitch determines its written note by going up a perfect fifth. F3 written is C4, because a fifth above F is C. F4 written is C5. C5 written is G5, because a fifth above C is G. F5 written is C6. Each of those pairs can be checked by the note numbers, which differ by 7 in every case: C4 at 60 to F3 at 53, C5 at 72 to F4 at 65, G5 at 79 to C5 at 72, and C6 at 84 to F5 at 77. The pattern in the partial numbers explains the shape of the answer, since a brass tube sounds its fundamental, its octave, its twelfth and its double octave, and those intervals are the ones the harmonic series produces at partial numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4. The written result is therefore the sequence C, C, G, C rather than a scale, and that irregularity is exactly what makes brass fingering worth learning. The trap in the first option is the natural one of writing down the sounding pitches, which would produce a part no horn player could read.
questions.hint: Go up a perfect fifth from each sounding pitch to find the written note, since a horn in F sounds a fifth below its part.

questions.topic: Which written notes in different parts sound the same pitch
questions.learningObjective: compare sounding pitches across several transposing parts
questions.stem: Four pairs of written notes are taken from an orchestral score in 4/4, common time, in c major. Which of the four statements about their sounding pitches is true? Select every statement that holds.

options.text: A horn in F written on C4 and an english horn in F written on C4 both sound F3, since both instruments are in F and both fall a perfect fifth
A bass clarinet in B flat written on D4 and a double bass written on C4 both sound C3, since the bass clarinet adds an octave to its whole-tone fall and the double bass falls one octave
A horn in F written on F3 and a trumpet in B flat written on C4 both sound Bb2, since a horn in F sounds a fifth below and a trumpet in B flat sounds a tone below
options.misconception: overlooks the octave difference between Bb2 and Bb3

options.text: A clarinet in B flat written on C4 and a bass clarinet in B flat written on C4 both sound Bb3, since both instruments fall a whole tone from their written pitch
options.misconception: forgets that a bass clarinet falls an extra octave

questions.explanation: Each pair has to be converted twice, once per instrument, before the two results can be compared. A horn in F and an english horn in F are both in F, so both take a written C4 down a perfect fifth to F3, and the two agree exactly, which is why the same written note serves both parts and no doubling is needed in the score. A bass clarinet in B flat falls a tone and an octave, so its written D4 becomes C3, while a double bass falls one octave, so its written C4 also becomes C3, and those agree too. The two false statements fail on the octave. A horn in F written on F3 sounds Bb2, but a trumpet in B flat written on C4 sounds Bb3, and Bb2 and Bb3 are an octave apart rather than the same pitch. A clarinet in B flat written on C4 sounds Bb3, but a bass clarinet written on C4 sounds Bb2, again an octave apart. The key check separates the two kinds of statement neatly, because the sounding pitches of the two true pairs are F3 and C3, both members of c major, which carries no accidentals at all, while the sounding pitches of the two false pairs are Bb2 and Bb3, and a B flat is not a member of c major. Both false statements share one root error, and it is the real one in score reading: the visible variety of a score is mostly in the notation, and a pair of parts that look different can produce exactly the same pitch while a pair that look alike can produce pitches an octave apart.
questions.hint: Convert both notes of each pair to their sounding pitches, then check whether the two results are the same pitch or an octave apart.

questions.topic: The order of staves in a full orchestral score
questions.learningObjective: read the vertical layout of a full score from the top down
questions.stem: A full score is laid out as a vertical stack of five staves, one per section, and the layout is given in full here. From the top of the page downward, staff 1 is flutes, staff 2 is oboes, staff 3 is clarinets in B flat, staff 4 is horns in F and staff 5 is bassoons. Every staff carries the same key signature, written in the concert key, and the two transposing staves are staff 3 and staff 4. Which staff carries the written key signature a whole tone higher than the others, and why is the stack ordered the way it is?

options.text: Staff 4, the horns in F, carries the written signature a whole tone higher, because an F part is notated a fifth above sounding and a fifth is the smallest such lift
options.misconception: picks the F staff and mistakes a fifth for a tone

options.text: Staff 3, the clarinets in B flat, carries the written signature a whole tone higher, and the stack is ordered by pitch height from the highest instrument down to the lowest
options.misconception: keeps the right staff but explains the order as pitch rather than seating

options.text: Staff 3, the clarinets in B flat, carries the written signature a whole tone higher, because a B flat part is notated a tone above sounding, and the stack runs woodwinds above brass and percussion above both because that is the seating order of the players
No staff carries a different written signature, because a full score prints every part in the concert key so that a reader can check the harmony directly
options.misconception: believes full scores print all parts at concert pitch

questions.explanation: Two separate conventions are at work in the layout, and the question separates them. The first is the written key signature. A part in B flat is notated a whole tone above sounding, so if the concert key is f major the clarinet part is written in g major and carries one sharp where the other staves carry one flat. A part in F is notated a perfect fifth above sounding, so the horn part is written in c major, a fifth above f major, and carries no accidentals. Both of those are staff 3 and staff 4, and the whole tone is the smaller of the two lifts, so staff 3 is the one a tone higher. The second convention is the vertical order, which follows the seating of the players in the hall rather than their pitch: woodwind and string families sit at the front and are written at the top, brass sit behind them, and percussion and voices, where present, are written at the bottom. The consequence for a reader is that the outer staves of a full score do not carry the extremes of the music, and the trap in the fourth option misstates the whole practice, since printing every part at concert pitch would defeat the purpose of the transposing part.
questions.hint: A B flat part is written a tone above sounding, and a full score is stacked in the players seating order.

questions.topic: A claim about a transposing part that the written note contradicts
questions.learningObjective: test a claim about a part against the pitches actually written
questions.stem: A copyist claims that a B flat clarinet part written in 4/4, common time, in g major sounds in g major as well, because the part and the orchestra differ only by an octave and octave transposition leaves the key alone. The bar holds a written F#5 quarter note, a written G5 quarter note and a written A5 quarter note, which fill it. Are the three written notes diatonic to g major, and what do they actually sound?

options.text: All three written notes are in g major, and they sound E5, F5 and G5, which are still in g major because an octave apart notes cannot change key
options.misconception: keeps the wrong sounding pitches and repeats the octave claim

options.text: All three written notes are in g major, and they sound E5, F5 and G5, which are members of f major, so the claim is false because a B flat transposition shifts by a whole tone and not by an octave
The written F#5 is the only diatonic note, and the G5 and A5 must be respelled, so the part is really in a key with three sharps
options.misconception: rejects two diatonic notes on a false respelling argument

options.text: All three written notes are in g major, and they sound F#5, G5 and A5, so the claim is true and the clarinet is a non-transposing instrument in this movement
options.misconception: ignores the B flat naming and accepts the claim

questions.explanation: The claim is testable in two steps and it fails the second. First the written notes: g major has one sharp, and F#5, G5 and A5 all belong to that scale, with the F# carried by the signature and needing no accidental, and the three quarter notes fill the bar's four beats only if one of them lasts longer, so the bar arithmetic is worth noticing but does not affect the test. Second the sounding pitches: a B flat clarinet falls a whole tone, so F#5 sounds E5, G5 sounds F5 and A5 sounds G5. Those three are the members of f major, which has one flat, and f major is a whole tone below g major, exactly as the naming requires. So the part is written in g major and sounds in f major, and the claim fails. The error in the claim is a specific one worth naming: a B flat transposition is a whole tone, not an octave, and only an octave transposition would leave the key untouched, which is the sole case in which the copyist's reasoning would hold. The trap in the fourth option is what happens when the naming is simply overlooked, and it is the most common way a copyist's claim survives unchallenged.
questions.hint: Check the written notes against g major, then drop each a whole tone and check the results against f major.
